newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Canada agency questions low Argentine rating.
newsitem.headline: Canada agency questions low Argentine rating.

text.p: Canadian Bond Rating Service Inc (CBRS) suggested Wednesday that Argentina deserved higher credit ratings than it has.

"Argentina compares quite favorably with many East European countries. Ironically it is rated below them," Ihor Kots, the managing director of CBRS, told Reuters in an interview. "On the surface of it, there are some inconsistencies."
Kots said Argentina's economy has "quite favorable prospects. The Tequila crisis slowed the economy, but it seems things are coming back on track."
"The remarkable thing in Argentina is that the cancer of hyper-inflation has been gotten rid off."
That and a strong growth outlook makes Argentina look stronger than many Eastern European countries.

Kots and John Neysmith, the vice president of CBRS, are on a week-long visit to Buenos Aires after the Canadian agency entered into a joint venture with local rating agency Ratto-Humphreys earlier this year.
They are also meeting government officials to get a view on Argentina's economy.
Kots would not say whether or not his agency is going to assign a sovereign credit rating to Argentina. CBRS' only sovereign rating is Canada.

"(But) there seems to be a lot of confusion and need for clarification (on ratings of Argentina). There seems to be divergent views," he said. "Recently there has been tremendous interest in the CBRS' view."

Speculation and confusion about Argentina's credit worthiness has gripped local markets in recent months after Standard & Poor's first raised the country's long-term foreign currency rating to BB from BB minus in March.

That was followed last month by a change in the criteria used by S&P in rating corporates operating in dollarized economies, which resulted in the upgrade of several Argentine firms to BBB minus -- the lowest investment-grade rating.
ING Barings said in a report Tuesday that the upgrade of the Argentine corporates raised more questions than answers.

"To the extent that dollarization is a determinant of credit worthiness, it's a criterion that should be applied first and foremost to the sovereign -- not, as in this case, to corporates alone," said ING.
But Moody's Investors Service does not think Argentina's risk has fallen sufficiently to raise the rating, according to Moody's lead Argentina analyst Kristin Lindow.
The biggest challenges facing the country lie with the government, said Kots, pointing to the need for reforms of the labor market and greater fiscal efforts.

Kots said his agency had an interest in increasing participation in Argentina through the joint venture with Ratto-Humphrews because of the rising involvement by Canadian companies in Latin American oil, gas and pipeline projects.

He also pointed to the similarities between Argentina and Canada's economies as a point of mutual interest. The populations of the two countries are of a similar size and both have ample raw materials.
Until the Second World War, Argentina and Canada had very similar growth patterns, he said.
Kots said CBRS is largely a Canadian government rater, but it is "looking at international projects on a selective basis."
